utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours; good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday, the 15th of September, 2009, I would like to greet Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic without forgetting Mr. Coric, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet the Defence counsel, Mr. Scott, and his associate, as well as all the people assisting us today. I'd like to greet our witness who has just entered the courtroom, and I would like to welcome him. We shall start off with the cross-examination. On the 7th of May, 2009, the Trial Chamber had handed a decision down on a request for review of the request to certify the decision. On the 22nd of April, 2009, by which we stated that Stojic, Prlic, and Petkovic's Defence teams would have two hours altogether to cross-examine the witness. We discovered yesterday that the Stojic Defence team would have no questions, which means that Mr. Prlic and Mr. Petkovic can share these two hours between them. We have been told that Mrs. Alaburic would need an hour and 45 minutes, and Mr. Karnavas 45 minutes pursuant to our decision. Well, he told us something between 15 and 20 minutes, but two hours is two hours. It's not two hours and five minutes. You will have to abide by the time constraints, otherwise things run out of control, which leads on to other problems. Mrs. Alaburic I shall now give you the floor. You have given us your binder, which we now have.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning to you. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Jurcevic, good morning to you too. Dr. Jurcevic, I wanted to ask you questions on three groups of topics, the HVO army, the Bosniak political and military leadership, and a set of topics of general political nature, primarily about borders. But I would like to start with another topic, because His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you yesterday about your MA thesis, the Myth of Jasenovac, and then His Honour Judge Trechsel asked you if you, as a scholar, dealt -- had dealt with the crimes committed by Croats against citizens of other ethnic backgrounds, and it seemed to me that we did not deal with it to the end and now would I like to ask you some questions about Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones that are not in use please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about Jasenovac. Dr. Jurcevic, do you consider Jasenovac to be a concentration camp run by the authorities of the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be more precise, it was a labour -- a combination of labour camp and concentration camp. I have written about that in scholarly papers, and I have spoken publicly about that on several occasions and it was completely under the authority of the government of the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is it controversial in your opinion that Jews were the victims of the Jasenovac concentration camp. Or if you want me to put it that way, Jews too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jews, Serbs, Croats and others. Well, I've written that extensively in my papers. They are victims of the worst kinds of crimes and atrocities committed in the Jasenovac camp, and I never doubted or questioned that in any way directly or indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted you to explain to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not only about the Jasenovac camp. Whenever I have written about the NDH, the Independent State of Croatia, I always have stress that had those -- that this was a totalitarian state and when laypersons asked me, I always stressed that this was a criminal state and nobody who espouses humanist position can say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I -- I monitored your public speeches quite carefully. I think you also condemned the crimes committed by the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. It is one of the greatest criticism levelled against the government of the Independent State of Croatia, and the fact that this was done under the pressure of the Nazi Germany to a certain extent, well, that doesn't mean anything. It doesn't justify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I simply wanted to clarify that so that we don't have any doubts about your positions about Jasenovac. Dr. Jurcevic, do you know that proportionately the number of Croats was the highest among the partisans? When I say proportionally, I mean I'm referring to the number of Croat partisans in relation to the overall population of Croatia at the time; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the partisans in the second Yugoslavia, I would not like to single Croatia out because the units were moving from one area to another, in particular in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but when you look at the initial years up until 1943, speaking in general in Croatia and in Yugoslavia the largest -- there was the largest number of Croats both in the partisan movement and in the Communist movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to the topics that I prepared for your cross-examination. I hope that you have a set of documents that has been prepared for you. If not, I would then like to ask the usher to hand it over. Please look at the documents in the binder. The document is -- that is in particular -- or, rather, a separate document is a transcript of the testimony by Dr. Smilja Abramov in the Milosevic case before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English version here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. You always have the Croatian behind it. The first document regarding the HVO is the document 4D0355. 4D01355.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the first document.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have the session of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, right at the beginning. I thought that first you have all the English texts and then all the Croatian texts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You can just look at the tabs where you have the number of the document. That's 4D01355. And if you go further a couple of pages, you'll see the Croatian text. It's an interview with General Milivoj Petkovic published in Vecernji List in August 1994, in August 1994, when he was about to leave Herceg-Bosna, and I will be interested in some of his statements regarding -- well -- or, rather, in light of your expert report, Dr. Jurcevic. If you look at the end of the first column, the question and answer there --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to note that it's at the end of page 1 and the beginning of page 2 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When asked what was happening with the HVO in the 28 months that General Petkovic spent in Herceg-Bosna, the general responded and I quote: "We didn't start with an organised army. Those were just armed groups. In some areas they were larger. In other areas they were smaller. I was setting up the organisation, and the staff existed even before I came. I thought that this army had been organised, but during the fighting in Kupres, we could see what we had at our disposal. The formations were not strong enough, organised enough, and they were not connected, one with another. Each municipality had it's own army. Then we started the reorganisation by establishing brigades. There was opposition to that. We established operative zones because the Main Staff, with some 15 people, could not cope with all of that. The biggest problem was the quality of the personnel, because this area -- well, it is known that people from this area do not care for the army." These assessments by General Petkovic, do they correspond to what you state in your expert report about the characteristics of the effort to organise the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have not seen this document before, but everything that you've just read out, the quote fully corresponds to what I concluded in the part of my expert report that pertains to the HVO; but I added in my expert report, in addition to the weaknesses that are listed here, some other problems that are quite important, the bad quality of the personnel, lack of training of the personnel manning those units; and in particular there was a big problem, and we have a number of original documents speaking about that, various forms of nepotism or amoral nepotism where the civilian authorities, the HVO, and the units, there was this whole network of amoral nepotism and other forms of preferential behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that I will have some documents about what you've just told us about, and we can deal with that in greater detail with those documents. Now I would like you to look at the next statement by Mr. Petkovic. It's at page 2 of the translation, and, Dr. Jurcevic, it's in the middle of the second column. When asked what the HVO looked like in August 1994, whether it was a proper army or just the armed populous, General Petkovic says, and I quote: "The HVO is in transition. A lot of things need to be done to establish an army. We are working on turning the HVO into an army, at least in its best part, and those are the Guards Brigades. It will become an army once we have certain peacetime contingent and once we know what to do and how to do it. The rest will be a territorial component." Dr. Jurcevic, how would you comment on this statement by General Petkovic that in August 1994 the HVO was not yet a proper army and that it was still in the process of development?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is completely true, but I would like to add from the military point of view there is an important fact that I included in my expert report which I failed to mention a little while ago. There was a big problem in the HVO units because of their local connections. If they received an order to move from their area, there were great problems, a great deal of opposition, not only on the part of the whole of the unit but individuals also would oppose it because there was no chain of command and no structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, are you trying to say that the municipal units considered that it was their task to defend their municipality and that they would not gladly receive orders to go and defend the territory of Herceg-Bosna in some other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. As I was advised to yesterday, I object to the leading nature of this question. It's completely leading, suggests the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Dr. Jurcevic has already answered my question, so my question is just an effort to sum up his answer to my previous question. That's number one. Number two, I'm cross-examining Dr. Jurcevic, so I do have the right to ask leading questions. I am aware of the fact that the Trial Chamber, in the context of -- in the context of all the questions and answers, will give proper value to every answer provided by Dr. Jurcevic, including this question which was, indeed, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I was wondering whether before the hearing I should not make a statement on a personal note on this particular issue which comes up time and time again, leading question or not. After having thought about it I felt, well, I wouldn't say anything, but there it is again. It is right that you are currently in the cross-examination phase. When I look into this, a cross-examination is a moment after which the witness has answered a number of questions, and, therefore, the person cross-examining will try to square things according to his or her own view during the cross-examination, and in that case leading questions should not be put. I have already said on several occasions that the Judges are professional Judges, are able to assess an answer on the basis of the quality of the question. If the question is extremely leading and if the answer is included or inferred from the question, the probative value of such an answer will, of course, be less than a question which is a better question. Its probative value will be then much higher than that of a remotely controlled answer. This is in practical terms. Let me remind you that in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence nothing is stated on the issue of leading questions. So what is leading and what isn't is something which is being assessed in practical terms. If you want your question to be properly assessed by the Bench, you must be careful not to put a question which would enable you to infer the answer from the witness. You are a very professional lawyer. You're perfectly capable of doing this given that you have a lawyer for a great number of years, so I'm not concerned about that at all. Admittedly yesterday we did have a problem when Mr. Kovacic was putting questions, but I do remember that at the time he had said when he started off that he may be putting leading questions, and I naively thought that he would put questions without intervening with the answers; but it's very difficult to understand this afterwards, because it's difficult to assess what kind of questions will be put beforehand. So this is what I have to say. Let's avoid making too many objections. What is important is what General Petkovic actually said during this interview, how should it be interpreted, and the answer may, as I say, may be able to shed some light on this. I give you the floor right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for those guidelines. I'm going to withdraw my question, because Dr. Jurcevic, in fact, has answered my question already in responding to the previous question. All I wanted to do was to summarise it and to emphasise it, but if you consider that is not necessary, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The third element from this interview, Dr. Jurcevic, that I wanted to draw your attention to and also to the Trial Chamber, is to be found at the beginning of the fourth paragraph or column. In the English, it is on page 3, and the question relates to the poor results of the war with the Muslims. General Petkovic says that it is true that the results were bad, and then the journalist goes on to ask him the following question and says: "Weren't the Muslims a weaker adversary?" And General Petkovic's answer is as follows, and I quote: "They were not. The placement of the Croatian population -- the distribution of the Croatian population is such that we are in enclaves everywhere. The balance of forces was unfavourable, and we never prepared ourselves for a war against them. Everybody at a local level formed their own judgement according to the following principle: 'They will not go against us.' We have good relations with them. Instructions were given to Bugojno and Vares, but we did not want to start a conflict anywhere." And in this connection, two questions to you, Dr. Jurcevic. In this interview, General Petkovic claims that the Croats did not prepare themselves to go to war against the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that assertion correct to the best of your knowledge or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To all intents and purposes and judging by everything I used in my research which I have listed here, many other documentation that I list, too, confirm that thesis in full. They confirm what General Petkovic said in this interview in 1994 completely, both on a political level and with respect to people's mentalities, and there were instructions given to Bugojno and Vares as it says in the last sentence. Well, as he said, "They're not going to go against us because we have good relations with them." So I have personal experience there. With the Court's permission, I would like to expound on that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My late uncle and his family lived in Bugojno - on my mother's side, that is - and in late 1991 in the autumn when there was an all-out war in the Republic of Croatia and when all my information told me that there would certainly be a Serb aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, I went to my uncle to warn him and tell him that he should prepare for that advent. I went personally to tell him that because he was my uncle, and he explained to me what the situation was in a similar way. And he would say on friendly terms, "My dear Josip, the situation is different here than to what it is over there. There won't be any war here." So that's my personal experience and testimony about the mentality that prevailed in those parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There's another claim made by General Petkovic here that I think is important in these proceedings, that is to say that everybody at their local level formed their own judgement as to whether they would go to war against someone and with whom or looking at the specific situation in at a local environment. So does that claim correspond to your knowledge of events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way it follows from that, that is true, but it also follows from my previous answers, and particularly from the elaboration of what I said in my expert report, and many authors and, for example, Jovan Divjak and others who were act -- who were part of the Bosnian army, they confirmed this thesis that there was, indeed, continuity in certain areas where the relationships were almost ideal without any conflicts or clashes between the BH army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document now, 4D16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you address a document, I wanted to get back to a question which was put by Mrs. Alaburic by way of an introduction which set me thinking, and I was wondering whether this doesn't pose a problem. She asked you a question on the partisans, and you answered by saying that as far as you knew, the partisans were practically for the most part Croatian. I'm using the conditional tense, but I believe that in 1942, Marsal Tito said that most of the partisans were Serbs. At that time, I believe, 90 per cent of the partisans were made up of Serbs from Croatia and Serbs from Bosnia. There might a contradiction in what you told us with what other people have stated. I want my question to be very clear and unambiguous. Can you confirm that, according to you, the partisans were made up of Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I presented in summarised form, it follows and can be checked from -- on the basis of statistical data with regard to the number of partisan units and their structures which were published in detail in much of the literature during the existence of the second Yugoslavia including summarised statistics, collective statistics. So in simple terms what I said was correct, and there is an explanation for that. Until 1943 when the partisans began to burgeon and became a more massive movement - and their progress confirms that until 1943 at the level of Yugoslavia and the partisan movement - until 1943 was for the most part on the territory of the Independent State of Croatia, then the majority of the people within the partisans were Croats. Later on, in the final years of the war, in 1944 and 1945, once again judging by information, not my data but data published by Yugoslavia and its scientific circles related to that subject, that ratio, for a series of reasons which we needn't go into here, changed. I did not say that there were 80 or 90, but when you look at the list from top to bottom, there were, of course, Serbs from Croatia. There were Muslims and so on and so forth, but until 1944 and the -- 1943 and the capitulation of Italy in 1943, on the 8th of September, the greatest participation were the Croats, and on the territory of the Independent State of Croatia, there was a very brutal civil war going on which had an ideological background and another background.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jurcevic, perhaps we could clarify. When we're talking about absolute figures, absolute numbers, and when we're talking about relative figures or, rather, the share of something with respect to the total population, I have the feeling that Judge Antonetti was speaking about the absolute number, those facts and figures. So according to the absolute number, there would be more Serbs, but if you look at the share compared to the total population, then the participation of Croats was greater. So in the proportionate sense. Could you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. The explanation you've just given is quite true, not to take up time, and this can all be verified even in encyclopedias, military encyclopedias or some other lexicographic literature from the times of Yugoslavia, because there was a lot of research at the time on the topic, because certain information figures. Now, were the Yugoslav -- was the Yugoslav research correct? I don't want to go into that. I didn't check it out. I took over some of these figures from those research studies. I said I didn't verify them. I just took them over regardless of whether they were correct or not. And in relation of -- in -- with respect to the balance of forces. Now we broached the topic, that those ratios were probably correctly demonstrated and shown, but it's also probable that Yugoslav historiography inflated the power and numbers of the partisans during World War II.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well let's move on to the next document which is 4D1674, 4D1674, which is a report from the commander of the brigade from Livno, which was sent to the Defence Department and the Main Staff and the operative zone, and here the brigade commander, at the very beginning, states: "We are unable to carry out the order of the operative zone to send brigade units to Donji Vakuf, because this was -- would lead to further destabilisation of the Livno front line." Tell us, please, Dr. Jurcevic, is this part of the report what you were telling us a moment ago when you said that part of the units refused to leave its territory and go and defend the territory of some other municipality? Is that the document that actually bears out what you were telling us earlier on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a typical document in that sense where individual local units, and I would say not for the reasons that are stipulated here, destabilisation of the front as it says here, but that in most cases the reasons were what we've said earlier, the lack of hierarchy functioning, the impossibility for a centralised command of the army, especially when we looked at the local situation, local authorities, local HVO authorities and so on. They functioned in similar fashion, so that this problem, the problem of centralisation for administration in that area and organisation in that area, in the military sense in terms of command or in other areas, was a very great problem with respect to financing and everything else. And I'd like to draw your attention to a document which is the source document which I use in my expert report on page 114, for example. I don't know what the English page is, but anyway, it's a report a from the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and it is called the concluding balance sheet for 1993, and there it lists the basic difficulties and limitations which took place throughout 1993. And then it lists 18 limiting circumstances which substantiate this position. So it's an official report from the times of what was going on, and, among other things, it says the lack of a uniform, financing system, the self-financing of units through existing organs. So self-financing for the HVO units, then the lack of a military establishment in proper terms and the fact that units were being formed and reformed, established and re-established. So the official documents list 18 shortcomings with confirm that in 1993, one could not say that we were dealing with a unified army from hierarchical considerations to finance considerations and everything else set out here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, look at the fourth paragraph now, please, which speaks about the involvement of the Livno Brigade in the Vakuf area, and it says that there was the -- the threads of a conflict there with unforeseeable consequences and that the Muslim population of Livno was dissatisfied with the involvement of the HVO in Vakuf area as well as with the previous involvement and engagement of people Prozor, but it says that they managed to prevent a conflict in Livno itself. Now, how do you understand this portion with respect to the desires of the Livno Brigade to be engaged in action on the territory of other municipalities against the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I understand it within the context we have been discussing, so localism, local considerations and everything that that entails. And secondly, it shows that -- and this is what history showed before, that there were not -- that there was no animosity in relations, thus far, between the Muslim Bosniaks and the Croats before this period, in the 1990s, and particularly in Central Bosnia. We had some excellent examples of co-existence, multiculturalism, good neighbourly relations and the like under very difficult circumstances as they were during the Second World War and during the second Yugoslavia. So unfortunately, the things that happened in certain localities in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the 1990s put paid to that tradition, and I deal with that and speak about that in the final part of my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, two passages later, it says that there was particularly -- a particular dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the same document which is 4D1674, and it's the fourth paragraph. It says: "People in Livno are particularly displeased that other municipalities of the operative zone and the -- the community of Herceg-Bosna, in general, are not participating in this patriotic war in accordance with their human and material resources, and why should Livno bear the greatest burden in this war?" Now, may we have your comments, Dr. Jurcevic, about this assertion of the people of Livno's dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is typical, and I quote another document in my expert report taken from Tomislavgrad wherein this local perception, the popular local perception, was that local communities were the centre of the world, if I can paraphrase in a sort of psychological sense what people thought, and that they bore the greatest burden and that nobody else was doing anything. And this is borne out by the lack of hierarchy and connection and lack of information, the flow of information, and intercommunity sentiments generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at the next document, which is 4D1298, and it is a document which the assistant head of the Defence Department for security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the document we have here on the screen was written on February 13, 1993, by commander -- by the brigade commander Stanko Vrgoc. When he wrote this document, I'm sure he had no idea that later in time international Judges would be scrutinising it. So given this, a priori, this document seems to be reflecting some kind of truth. And when you look into this document, the impression that any reasonable trier of fact could get, of course everybody is entitled to their own opinion, but when you read this document, you feel that the author is really saying what the Croats from Livno are thinking. He's just saying that there's a problem with all the Muslims that came into Livno, that there's 7.500 Muslims that came into Livno. He said that in the units there are almost 33 per cent Muslims, and he also explains that there's a front line and that units should be sent to this front line and not elsewhere. And then maybe he's a bit ironic, I don't know, but in the end, he ends his letter with a military salute with many exclamation marks. So maybe this commander from Livno -- he's talking about a conflict between Muslims and -- and the Croats, but he's not talking about any aggression, but he obviously is putting forth local interest before anything, notably as far as -- as far as what's happening in Livno is concerned. I don't know if you had already seen this document, but I would like to know whether you've seen other documents of the like which would prove or demonstrate that in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the main point was the defence of local communal interests rather than defending the homeland. People were caring about their own town, their own settlement more than anything and the rest was secondary. Would you give us your take on this, notably since you told us earlier that you went to Bugojno to see your uncle. So you have a first-hand experience on this. Can you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I believe that you -- that your statement is very accurate. This hierarchy from the relationship between the greater whole and the local unit was actually upside down. I think that what you said is correct on the basis of my own experience, analysis, and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second question now: This document will be used by the Judges, you can be sure of that, and in the second paragraph there is a passage that might be a bit problematic. It seems that there is a coordination of the Croatian army, the HVO. Livno is at the border of Croatia. So is it because of its geographical situation that there is mention of this coordination between the two forces, and if such coordination did exist, could you tell us exactly what kind of shape it had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to a whole series of documents - I quoted some of them by way of illustration in my expert report - according to the plans and the implement of the Serbian aggression both against the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territory of the two states, regardless of the borders, so before and after the international recognition of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, was treated as a single theatre of war. Some of the documents are incorporated in the expert report, so that the organisation of the defence in the area of Croatian Community or Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and before that in large parts of the Republic of Croatia depended on the local situation. Since the area of Livno and southern parts of that area and of Croatia were of extreme importance for the Serbian aggression, one of the rare facts that is really prominent among what we know about that period is that one of the key, if not the key, goals of the Serbian aggression was to take as much of the Adriatic coast as possible. That meant, for the most part, large parts of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, the axes of the attacks and the efforts to cut Croatia into two parts around Ston, in the Zadar hinterland, and the other plans that followed the Neretva River valley went from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the Republic of Croatia. So any kind of co-operation, strategic, military, between the HVO and the HV was logical in a way and was, in fact, dictated by the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, could you please tell us whether the municipality of Livno borders with the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the broader Livno area does border with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when the Army of Republika Srpska or any other aggressor wanted to go from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, could you answer precisely. The question was whether the municipality borders. Your answer is whether the -- that the broader area does border. Can you answer the question as it was put? Does the municipality have a common border with Croatia, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood the doctor to be speaking about the broader area of the town of Livno and was not aware of the -- all the details about the borderline.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if the Republika Srpska army or anyone else wanted to attack from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the Republic of Croatia in the area of Central Dalmatia, what would be the logical step to take? Would they pass through the Livno municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly that is how it is, and some plans of the Serbian army or JNA elements that were in effect, the Serbian army testified to that. They drafted and implemented those plans in the course of the aggression against the Republic of Croatia. I stressed that they treated that as a single theatre of war. A number of indicators showed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, it is only then logical to conclude that the Livno Brigade, by defending the Livno municipality and its territory, was, in effect, in a way defending the Republic of Croatia in that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Objection. Leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will ask this leading question and it's up to you to decide whether it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, without avoiding the problem of the leading question, you could just have asked the following question: Professor, you said you looked at attack -- Serbian attack plans. Could you tell us what the strategic objective was for the Serbs, and, as an answer, he would have said the objective was to attack the Republic of Croatia through Livno in order to occupy Dalmatia, and because this would jeopardise the Republic of Croatia. You would have ended up exactly with the same answer. You elicited exactly what you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but let me just say one thing. If I were to ask this kind of question and expect an answer, to my mind, this question would imply that the Livno Brigade was defending the Livno territory in order to defend the Republic of Croatia against potential Serbian aggression. But that is not my question. It is my question -- well, it's related to the segment that you quoted in this element, the defence of Herceg-Bosna on its western borders and the defence of the territory of the Republic of Croatia south of the Dinara. So my question s pertain only to that document. I didn't want to ask any questions, but I wanted to follow up on your questions because I thought it needed to be cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this builds on the issue I raised at the end of the day yesterday, and, again, I remind everyone that I was chastised for not making individual objections. So that's what I'm going to do. The point is this: When a witness is asked an open-ended question, the witness has to give a full answer and has to give some sort of, presumably, a basis for the answer, not simply yes or no. And there were many instances yesterday where there were leading questions where the witness did very little more than say yes or no. Yes, that's right; yes, that's right; yes, that's right. That is not helpful to the Chamber or to the Prosecution in the sense of knowing the basis of his testimony on what basis he says that, what is -- what is reasons for what evidence he's looked at. It's just simply a yes answer, and I continue in the position I stated yesterday. And I would ask that the -- I would ask the Chamber also inquires into these things. When the witness says these things, what's the basis for having him say it other than just voicing a bald opinion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, I do want to say something because I think that we're now -- I'm, at least, extremely disturbed by the way this Trial Chamber is approaching the Defence as being one conglomerate, one mono-ethic entity, and we're all being lumped together, at least that's what would occur if I understand the President's comments correctly. Because if the President seems to be suggesting that we should all be conducting direct examination through somebody else's Defence, and that's not appropriate. Now, if that's not the letter and spirit of Judge Antonetti's remarks, then it would appear that Mr. Scott is in error, because Mr. Scott wishes to treat all the Defence as if we're all conducting direct examination, and, therefore, we all have to ask open-ended questions. I do agree with the gentleman. Yesterday there was a some leading. I don't want to be associated with that leading, that has nothing to do with me, but when I stand up to do cross-examination, I'm entitled to ask leading questions, a question that suggestion the answer. And if I need to ask for additional explanations, I will do so; but I should not be compelled to ask open-ended questions during cross-examination. Now, I understand there maybe some instances where I'm going outside the scope of the direct, and I'm trying to elicit positive information, and in those instances, as we've had this discussion based on a rule inspired by the Federal Rules of Evidence, I may be compelled to ask an open-ended question because, after all, I'm asking for new information outside the scope. But if I'm doing cross-examination in a classical sense, I should be entitled to ask leading questions. So I don't think that this is a well-founded objection on behalf of the Prosecutor. But I also think he has every right to object, and as he does object, as when we do object, he's entitled to a decision and ruling from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may very briefly. My colleague has been raising an issue that actually was initially raised yesterday. I didn't want to take the floor yesterday. I thought his objections were completely groundless, but I would like to remind you of one thing. This is not an Anglo-Saxon courtroom, and as you, Your Honour, noted a little while ago, our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the official rules in force here, have -- impose no further restriction on direct -- on examination-in-chief and cross-examination apart from just listing all types of examination. So case law actually gives us guidance. As my learned friend Mr. Karnavas has just noted, and this is what my learned friend Ken Scott has been saying, well, we don't have the Federal Rules of Evidence here. I'm not going into why we don't have them. If we don't apply one set of rules contained therein, we cannot apply any other rules from there. What I'm trying to say is there are different rules that apply to examination-in-chief of expert witnesses who have come here with an expert report that everybody has read. And here the questions on leading are different than they are with fact witnesses. That's how it is in continental law. It's one thing to ask questions about the expert report that we all have, and it's a different thing when you ask questions that are not based on any such material; and I think that the expeditiousness of the proceedings is critical, and it is gaining in importance every day. So this is a tool that enables us to question witnesses more quickly. So if my colleague had some objections yesterday to leading questions in the examination-in-chief, regardless of the fact that we had an expert report, he had to take the floor immediately because he is sticking to the rules that prevail in an Anglo-Saxon courtroom and this is not it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, before I give you the floor, I would like to remind everyone that the Trial Chamber issues guidelines on this issue. Of course the Judges have thought about all this, all these problems that crop up all the time. In the decision of April 24, 2008, we said the following: "When a topic has already been dealt with during direct examination, leading questions are allowed." When, however, a new topic is being dealt with, a topic which was not mentioned during the direct examination, the Trial Chamber said that this is now a direct examination and not a cross-examination and that, therefore, leading questions are not allowed. It's guideline number 3, paragraph 8. Everything is in the guidelines. So the only problem is the following: When the question is being put, is it a new topic? Yes or no? And all the rest is just posturing and nothing else. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Karnavas and I are in partial agreement on several points this morning. He said something that was very important, and that was -- and I agree with him, in a classical example of cross-examination where the evidence of a witness is being challenged, in a classical cross-examination, the witness is being tested, that is one thing. Leading questions are fully appropriate, and I certainly agree with that. Again, Your Honour, what I submit is happening now is this is nothing more than a common witness. This is nothing more than a common witness. Ms. Alaburic is not testing the evidence of this witness at all. She's not challenging this witness or his evidence, she's simply continuing a direct examination; and that directly impacts the Prosecution because the Chamber is not giving me any additional time to respond to her questions and it's just a continue -- and I don't blame her for that, but it's a continuing direct examination of what is, for all practical purposes, a common witness. She has not challenged the witness once, Well, witness, you said this, I put it to you the opposite. Witness, you said this, I put it to you the opposite, Witness. Witness you said this, I'm impeaching you with your prior statement. There is not any of that. This is a continuation of friendly questions on a direct examination nature, in which leading questions are not appropriate, and the Prosecution should have time to respond to it. And that continues to be our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going to respond to what me learned friend Mr. Scott has just said because that what he says almost every time when he gets up to react to the cross-examination of Defence teams. Now, the Trial Chamber has made a ruling in the matter, and I don't think we need deal with the comments made by my learned friend Mr. Scott. Now, I'd like to stress that all the Defence teams have the right to conduct a cross-examination related to all parts of the expert report by Dr. Jurcevic, regardless of the fact of whether they -- the -- their colleagues in the Praljak Defence had time during the examination-in-chief to emphasise one point or another. So I can use my cross-examination and base it on the parts of the expert report that Mr. Kovacic did not deal with. That does not mean that I will step beyond the topics of the examination-in-chief. And the next thing I'd like to say, with respect to new topics in the cross-examination, is that the Petkovic Defence considers that every topic which is broached by the Judges when they ask their questions become a topic relevant for cross-examination and cannot be considered to be a new topic introduced. Now, since Judge Antonetti mentioned -- the mention of the Croatian Army in the second portion of the document we discussed, I considered it my duty to expound that topic fully through my questions to show that it was not a question of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina but the Croatian army is mentioned in quite a different context. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can move on to the next document, then, Dr. Jurcevic, it is document 4D1298 that I'd like to deal with now. 1298 is the next document, and it is a document which the assistant head of the Defence Department sends in September 1993 to the head of the Defence Department. And it is information about the thoughts and behaviour of the inhabitants of Livno, in terms of relations between Herceg-Bosna and the municipality. So the inhabitants of Livno vis-a-vis the relations between the HB and the municipality. And I'd like to point out some of the thoughts here. They say that they're not much interested in Herceg-Bosna, that they are excessively concerned about their municipality. Secondly, that their patriotism only extends to the Municipal Boarders and that they feel no need to fight any further. Then that they do not agree with the decision of the Main Staff to transfer pieces to the active front. Next, that they are protesting against mobilisation and taking away their machines for the building of roads, and finally, that all artillery pieces and weapons are considered by them to be the property of Livno and that they can, therefore, not be transferred to other fronts even by an order from the General Staff. Now, Dr. Jurcevic, may we have your comments to that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is another typical document which confirms what I said earlier on and -- the points we touched upon and which I deal with in my expert report. Or, in other words, it is precisely the way Their Honours asked me questions about this, looking at it from different aspects and different sides. These documents bear all that out, that is to say that the local community, whether it be Livno or any other local community, was primary for the population, both in the military and political sense. And this report, dating back to those times of a body of central authority, indubitably confirms what we said at all levels. And I would like to reiterate what His Honour the Judge said that this kind of patriotism and all other responsibilities are only seen as responsibilities towards one's local community, and it is clear from what was latterly stated there as considered to be something quite normal. And they consider it quite normal to reject orders from the Main Staff which one cannot even conceive of let alone write something down in a well-structured and organised state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, Doctor, which is 4D1328. 1328 is the document number. 4D1328. Yes, it's correct number now. This is a letter of resignation sent to Anto Roso, General Anto Roso, commander of the HVO Main Staff in December 1993, and it says that the resignation has been made because of those people and a group of powerful men who are deeply rooted behind the back of the command of the brigade of which I had been charge until this resignation. It is increasingly important to those group of people - I will repeat the last sentence - to these people and to this group of powerful men, everything else is more important, war profiteering and local rivalry more important than the defence of the homeland. Dr. Jurcevic may we have your comments to that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again a typical document confirming everything we've said so far, and, in a way, it correctly defines the situation. When we look at it from a politicological aspect and sociological aspect, that is to say when you are witnessing the disintegration of one system without another system being established. So it's a deep institutional crisis that is afoot, and all the negative facets of that come to the fore here, selfishness, crimes, corruption, nepotism, amoral nepotism; that I have already set out when I spoke about the Croatian Community and its shortcomings, and it's the same in my conclusions when we're talking about the Croatian Community -- or, rather, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and on the basis of a whole series of documents of -- of this type, I summarise it all and set out the conclusions and consider them to be the lack of quality or the shortcomings that existed. And this document is testimony to the realistic state of affairs in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna both in the civilian area and the military sector of life and work; that is to say some institutions have disappeared because of the situation the BH was facing, new institutions are trying to be established but without success, or very little success. Because as you yourself stressed, we're dealing with December 1993 here, which means that a lot of time has gone by since the decision was made to establish a Croatian Community; that is to say two years on, a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, so during those two years, quite obviously, not even the initial problems of establishment for the system both civil and military were actually functioning property regardless of the fact that in the Narodni List and the Official Gazette, if you looked at this, everything looked hunky-dory, everything made you think that there was an organisation with a proper hierarchy and so on. But in analysing the documents, there was still a lot of disarray and that was the main characteristic and this was the consequence of the general situation that existed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Dr. Jurcevic, in your report -- in part of your report, you write about the doctrine of total national defence and social self-protection or All People's Defence and social self-protection and that is to be found in section 131, para 312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you address that, Professor, when I put the question to you earlier on, I did not know of the existence of these two documents because I hadn't looked at them. I look at one document after another, so my question had not factored in this document. Now that you have this document, I would have put you the same question, but now I'm asking you for additional information. You said a few moments ago that everything was in disarray. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the translation was, but what I said was that it was a typical situation when one institution -- when institutions in an area actually cease to exist and others were trying to be established but had for the been established yet. And as you said, it was, in lay terms, chaos, and in a scholarly sense the restructuring of the system. So your previous question, although you said that you hadn't seen the document, was probably on the basis of other documents that you've seen during this trial and that led you to make the conclusion that I wholly corroborated and said was correct, and I came to that conclusion on the basis of my own research. So I agree with you that it was a repercussion of the fact that the local community was being seen as the be-all and end-all for everybody's interest and that was just one consequence of the overall situation in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Dr. Jurcevic, I wanted to ask you several questions on the doctrine of total national defence and social self-protection, and you write about this in your expert report. You say that it is the document developed in a period from 1969 onwards to 1974. Now, do you know what events led to the creation of this concept of All People's National Defence? What happened, for example, one year earlier on a world level in 1968?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the events in Czechoslovakia to which you're probably alluding to where the Soviets made a military intervention and the international reasons for the establishment -- the international reasons for setting up the All People's Defence and social self-protection system, that was one of the causes, but there were other reasons, the crisis within the second Yugoslavia and that crisis loomed five or six years earlier; that is to say from 1965 onwards, the second Yugoslavia, for the first time because of the social and economic crisis, it opens its borders for the first time and many of its citizens went to work abroad. In 1966, there was a settling of accounts internally which was known as the Tito Rankovic clash. Rankovic was the chief of police and chief of the intelligence services, the secret services. And in 1967, then, when it was about Croatia, there was a declaration about Croatian literary language which led to a great storm and was claimed to be a counter revolution and hostile action. And if you add to this 1968 in Czechoslovakia then this same international reason, that is to say a fear that the Soviet Union under certain circumstances might intervene in Yugoslavia as well, all that in addition to everything else, were reasons to form this concept of All People's Defence and social self-protection, and I quote here experts, Yugoslav experts, who wrote the history of Yugoslavia and the history of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia who said themselves that this concept was established and I quote: "In the spirit of Marx's concept of an armed people and that every part of Yugoslavia should be a front line and each of its citizens a warrior, a fighter." And I quote the source, so that is taken from the 1974 constitution, that is to say this concept, as I quote it, began to be established in 1969 and was ultimately formulated in the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Dr. Jurcevic, if you can remember, in the former Yugoslavia how hold were we when we were trained for defence? The citizens. How was a citizen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, symbolically from birth, I would say. That is to say in primary school there was what was called -- well, at different levels, too, at secondary school and at university we had sort of pre-military training. That's what it was called. And that was a subject taught by some professionals who had completed studies in All People's Defence and social self-protection, and then there was certain civil protection drives and other ones that were called NNI. That is to say an abbreviation for nothing must be allowed to take us by surprise in translation, where the citizens had to take part in certain, well, I would say, nonsensical drives. And just to show you the absurdity of it all of one such drive that took place -- or, rather, was proclaimed to take place in Split in the media, and then when the day came to hold that drive, nothing must take us by surprised as it was titled, the papers wrote that the action or drive was postponed -- was going to be postponed because of rain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned this training. In all socially owned companies and state institutions, were people also trained in the area of All People's Defence and self-protection? Do you have any knowledge about that? What happened in the socially owned enterprises, state institutions, and so on and so forth, other services?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essential part of this concept in the armed sense was the Territorial Defence, which was a form of republican army. We can call it that, in the sense of co-ordination and command. And I'm going to quote, once again, the constitution. It's a brief quote for us to be able to understand what this is was all about; this is what it says, including the whole economic system, administrative system, now I come to the 1974 constitution, quote, the Yugoslav constitution: "It is the right and duty of the municipalities of the autonomous provinces of the republics and all other socio-political communities each in its -- and on its territory to set up and organise national defence and to be in charge of territorial defence, civilian protection, and other preparations for the defence of the country."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, do you know about Zagreb, the courses in All People's Defence? At what faculty were they organised and run, this whole course of studies?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Faculty of Political Science in Zagreb, there was a special course of study, All People's Defence and social self-protection. I studied social sciences at the time, so I know how it was very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And do you know when did -- when were the first students enrolled in this course? In All People's Defence. Well, it's not important. It's was in --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was in 1975. Please look at 4D1603. 4D1603. It's a document from the BH army, the guidelines for fostering and boosting combat morale in the BH army, and I would like to discuss this with you in this context, the concept of defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina as such. In item 1 of this document, the unity of all the components of armed struggle and resistance, it speaks about unity of all the components; on the one hand, the armed struggle, and on the one hand and resistance on the other. So we have two elements of the defence. And in the second paragraph, I will read this out: "Special importance for the fostering and boosting of the combat morale lies in the unit of the army and the people based on the traditions of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its people. It is boosted and built up on all forms of joint preparations of the army and the people for the defence of the country." And now I will skip four lines, and I will continue with my quote: "And overall efforts and the assistance of the people to the army expressed through material support, caring for the wounded and the sick, gathering information about the enemy, uncovering and obstructing enemy agents, provocateurs and saboteurs in the field -- provocateurs and saboteurs in the field, securing important features and supply sources, participation in the fortification of the terrain and other activities." Doctor, tell us whether the struggle of the army and the people defined in this manner is, in fact, an implementation of the doctrine of the All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's one of the minor forms described here of the whole system of the All People's Defence and social self-protection. There is a whole number of other elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to move on to the topic whether, and to what extent, the Muslim political and military leadership supported the Vance-Owen Plan and other peace plans put forward by the international community. We will skip one document, and we will go to document 4D1235. 4D1235. It's a document dated 10th of January, 1993, and it is sent by the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. It is a press release or an announcement on the subject of the talks in Geneva, and the commander of the 3rd Corps says: "On the occasion of the continuation of the political negotiations in Geneva and on the request of a huge number of units and fighters of the 3rd Corps of the BH army, we hereby offer you our unconditional support in your efforts to prevent the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina on ethnic or any other principle." Dr. Jurcevic, could you please comment on this document in the context of the peace talks in Geneva? It is part of your expert report. And the proposal that was on the table at the time that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be divided into ten cantons which would be set up primarily but not exclusively on ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan, before the draft was made public, right at the beginning of 1993, had been in the process of drafting for several months. And the public was aware of the fact that it would involve the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into ten or to seven provinces, and this is a response to this document. Now, whether it was spontaneous or organised, well, I don't know that when it comes to this document, but all peace plans caused major response at all levels of government and also at the international level, because those plans dramatically changed the principles, the approach to Bosnia and Herzegovina as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at our next document, 4D76. It's a -- it's a document from February 1993. It's a report sent by the IPD of the 4th Corps to the brigades which are part of that corps, and here an interpretation of the Geneva and New York talks is provided. In item 1 it says, and I quote: "The active involvement of the USA in the Vance-Owen negotiations represents a qualitative shift for the better with regard to increasing pressure on the aggressor ..." And then in item 2 it says: "European countries and the USA do not intend to engage militarily in the theatre of operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the foreseeable future, and for as long as in their assessment there is any chance of ending the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina by diplomatic means." And then in item 4: "Expecting that there would be -- any kind of external solution could have a negative influence on the combat morale of members of the BH army, which is why, in the carrying out their daily tasks, all members, commanders and Staffs of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina must take an active stand towards the obligations of the armed struggle. Any lulls in combat operations should be used for high-quality preparations for carrying out further operations." Now, Dr. Jurcevic, I would like us to comment a little bit on this document, in particular in the item 2 where it says that the European countries and the USA do not intend to engage militarily in Bosnia and Herzegovina for as long as there is any chance of ending the conflict by diplomatic means. How do you interpret this assessment by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it followed from the experiences until that time, and it was obvious, as we said yesterday, that any peace plan put forward by the international community could not be implemented, had to be imposed. On the other hand, the other developments, in particular, in 1992, in the second half of 1993, the international developments confirmed this position. The international conference produced a large number of papers with great promises, a lot of talk, but nothing happened. The Serbian armed aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina kept escalating. So this is one of the documents, this paragraph 2, I think, is based on the experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, to the best of your knowledge, did the Muslim political and military leadership actually want the European countries and the USA to intervene militarily?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this follows from their demands. Yesterday I said that as early as 1991 Alija Izetbegovic and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had started launching appeals for observers to be deployed. And in 1992 there was a whole series of appeals, demands, and so on. In this period and even before that and after, that there was a continuity and it is quite logical for the weaker side, and the central government in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the weaker side, the Muslim, Bosniak and Croat structure, in other words, and they wanted, they wished for and they appeal for an international military intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, a military intervention and diplomatic means are mentioned in item 2. What is your conclusion? At what point it is realistically to expect the European countries and the USA to intervene in Bosnia and Herzegovina based on item 2? What would follow from item 2? When would it be realistic to expect their military involvement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you personally, but what do you conclude --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, please slow down. The interpreters are begging for mercy. You're going way too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm not asking for your personal opinion, but I'm just asking you what did the drafter of item 2 think on the basis of this item 2? What is it that follows from this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what follows from this document is what is explicitly stated here that this is not expected in the foreseeable future, any time soon, and for as long as there is a possibility of achieving a diplomatic solution, but that's a very undefined term and it can go on forever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it is time for our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you have 45 to 50 minutes left. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did Jurcevic, we will dwell a little bit more on the documents from the Bosniak Muslim side in the conflict, because I believe that it might assist us to better understand the moves the Croatian side. Could we please look at 4D766. It's a proposal of measures to organise the All People's liberation war, which in May 1993, was drafted by the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to draw your attention to some parts thereof, and I would like you to comment on them. In the second paragraph it says, and I quote: "The radical U-turn in the attitude of the great powers to aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina clearly shows that the defence of the state and of the people must be organised and conducted by relying on our own forces. Compared to the situation and conduct so far, this implies a total and final dispelling of all illusions about any possible external military intervention as a decisive factor in putting a stop to the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and a switch to the wartime model which implies maximum mobilisation of all the segments and the entire potential of the state for its survival." Dr. Jurcevic, can you comment on it in the context of perhaps some strategic decisions taken by the Bosniak Muslim side in the conflict? Microphone for the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it follows from this that there is no expectation, or they no longer expected the international community to intervene militarily in any way and that the structures of the Bosniak Muslims in the central government should now concentrate on the wartime model, should switch over to the wartime model.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at the first little line on page 1 for you. In the English it's on the second page. So the proposals. Let me quote: "In the crucial moment to mobilise and unite all political forces, parties, associations, movements and citizens into a patriotic front, and replacing the strategy that was pursued so far of being victims and seeking internal aid on that basis, to develop a strong combat morale relying on our own forces and providing support to the BH Army in its struggle for the defence of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our country and salvation of our people in the face of new pogroms." Doctor, I would like to ask you to comment on the part of this quote that pertains to the strategy pursued so far, which was that of creating an image of victims and seeking external aid, the Bosniak Muslim leadership was building in its strategy regarding its relations with the international community and other warring factions on that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This strategy of turning oneself into a victim can be seen from what we look at the international perception in the media and elsewhere of the Bosniak Muslims in the previous period, the second half of 1992, in particular the first part of 1993, the first half of that year, because a lot of information was published in the media about camps, and the Muslim Bosniaks were in the focus in terms of diplomatic and media levels, and we have to note that this document was drafted immediately after they gave up -- or, rather, when the Vance-Owen Plan fell through after the referendum when the Serb side, on the 19th of May, announced its final decision renounce the plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in the context of this strategy of being a victim, on the second page, the longest paragraph, which deals with the Ministry of Information. It's at page 3 in the English version, and some activities on the part of the Ministry of Information of Bosnia and Herzegovina are hereby proposed, including radio and television, and then somewhere in the middle of the paragraph it says: "It is necessary to make sharp cut in the awareness of the people whom produce programmes and avoid the cliches when depicting the victims and the suffering, and avoiding the affirmation of our own army and our struggle for freedom." Can you -- Mr. Jurcevic, this qualification for the programme of state radio television as showing suffering, can you comment about that within the frameworks of the previous victims strategy that we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, in the institutions under the supervision of the structures of power and authority, that is to say the Muslim Bosniak majority, did have a strategy by way it waged a psychological war, if you will, towards the international community and tried to depict itself as a victim. Now, I'd like to emphasise the fact, and if he's not suitable tell me, but anyway, there was an internal conflict within the Muslim Bosniak structures themselves when it came to the BH Army because of something we called the Islamisation of the army. And in keeping with that, there were cadres changes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certain prominent individuals from the political life of the country. Rusmir Ahmet Cehajic, for example, didn't want to take part in that any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like now, Dr. Jurcevic, to look at some plans that the political leadership had, the Bosniak Muslim side, principally through the transcripts of the sessions of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In order to do that, look at 4D1118 now, please. And we'll start off with page 7 of the Croatian or Bosnian text, whatever you like to call it, which is in the English page -- the page ends in the following digits on e-court, 1446. Yes, 1446. The last paragraph on that page. Stjepan Kljujic says the following: "It is obvious that Geneva --" I apologise. I have to give the date of this session. It's the 26th of November, 1993. And Stjepan Kljujic says the following: "It is obvious that Geneva has to solve the question of humanitarian survival, and not only for this winter since the negotiations on Bosnia and Herzegovina could last for five years, to definitely deal with the question by force. And we have to insist there, and we have the support of Europe in at a regard." I'm going to skip over several lines there and continue. We must --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you be so kind and indicate exactly where you are? I have not found the quotation that you've read.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they have not either.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, we have established that it is not 1446 but 1147. So the following page. In the middle of the page, Stjepan Kljujic speaking. 1447 is the number. Let me repeat. Page 1447 for the English. If we've found it, I can continue quoting Stjepan Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He says: "We must form an action to prepare for the disavowment of Stoltenberg and Owen, and the formal thesis is the Geneva conference was not successful. A new conference is being prepared with the unsuccess of the Geneva principle, the mediators have to be withdrawn too." Now, Dr. Jurcevic, to the best of your knowledge, were there really some attempts made for Messrs. Stoltenberg and Owen to be thrown out as mediators in the negotiations, and do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today that is obvious from looking at the basic documents and the fate of the Stoltenberg-Owen Peace Plan which had the largest number of variants offered up, and the events themselves led to this; that is to say, when the conference on the former Yugoslavia died a natural death. After Washington, well that was the process. It was a process. And finally, the Contact Group was established led by the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to look at page 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go on, this is one where -- could we have a little basis for him saying this other than saying that the Owen-Stoltenberg talks came to an end? We know they came to an end, but this specific question was: Does he have knowledge that these men were somehow forced out, there was an effort, a campaign to remove them? I don't think that question was answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This could be a question for the cross. Witness, to save some time, could you tell us on what basis you're basing yourself to answer Mrs. Alaburic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of the events that we know about today, that we know happened, global events. So in April, the 25th of April, 1994, in actual fact, a Contact Group was established, and before that the United States of America intensively or -- became included evermore intensively in the processes evolving on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia sort of withered away, and the fate of the plan, the peace plan, which was known under the title of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, fluctuated or, rather, there were many versions of it, which meant that Owen and Stoltenberg were not accepted. So they had to change their variants often in keeping with the interests that obviously existed within the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, tell us, do you know whether some of the participation in these international negotiations published books about the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robert Owen did. He published a book, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you read the book?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. It was a long time ago, but when you read memoirs of this type, I always take them with a pin much of salt, with some reservations with respect to the facts, because the people taking part try to depict their role by asserting themselves, protecting themselves and their actions, justifying themselves and generally portraying themselves in a positive light.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to a particular portion of this transcript in which the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, sums up the agreements and how his delegation should act.
