On page 19 of the Croatian text, which is page 1459 of the English, Alija Izetbegovic is speaking and says: "We could come up with some conclusions for the time being. Let the delegation go up there. There is more or less, and we know what the platform is, plus those efforts regarding the expansion of functions and territories, plus the nonsignature, et cetera." Then on page 21, which is page 1461 of the English, the beginning of the second paragraph he says -- it is said: "Let's save what we can. We have the chance to expand the areas somewhat in which we have an opportunity to create democratic will." Then I'm going down to the end: "There, let the delegation go to Geneva with those thoughts in mind and let them try and say what can be saved, what they can." So in those portions, the ones I've quoted, it says that one of the guidelines to the delegation from the Presidency of the BH is not to sign any document. Dr. Jurcevic, do you have any knowledge about this strategic action on the part of the Bosnian Muslim side, that is to say take part in the negotiations but to refrain from signing any documents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically at the end of September the Bosnian -- Bosniak Muslim majority in the Assembly rejected the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, which led to a crisis within its ranks, the greatest crisis to date, which was evidenced in the departure of a member -- a Bosniak member of the Presidency, Mr. Fikret Abdic. He went to the western part of BH and set up an autonomous province there called Western Bosnia with all the consequences that this gave rise to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Unfortunately, I don't have time to ask you any additional questions because I want us to get through some more documents. The next one of which is 4D1052. And that is the transcript from a Presidency meeting of BH on the 29th of December, 1993. Doctor, take a look at page 8/2, which in the English version is a page ending in 0753.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 8/2 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a copy. What's the other page number?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't say now.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. 8/2. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me just place this in context. They are discussing an offensive by the BH Army in Central Bosnia, or more specifically in the Vitez area. So let's see what they say about that. Alija Izetbegovic, and I quote, says: "But in the discussions we had the previous night, he said," please, he's referring to Tudjman, "I hear you have an offensive underway against Central Bosnia. So please stop that offensive, and so on and so forth. And that is what he wrote in the letter, 'I told Vesnija [phoen] that there is no offensive. There's just a conflict over there where the armies are confronted and are fighting at Vitez and so on.'" Now, on the following page, it is 8/3, and in the English it's on the same page, Izetbegovic going on to say, and I quote: "I have not promised that we would stop anything except that this request for a Christmas truce came later and we accepted it, but we can only speak about a violation of that truce if there's something on our side. Otherwise, there are no other obligations." The end of the page Ganic, Ejup Ganic begins, which is on the following page, Your Honours, and the last digits on that page are 54, Ejup Ganic, and I'm going to precis what he says. He says that possibly a valve could be opened to Vitez and that the population should leave the area and to go to Boban. And now I'm going to quote another page on 9/3, which is page 0756 in the English. Kljujic is trying to advocate that Vitez should not be taken control of, and that is what Kljujic says: "Since they have accused us before the UN and because we must give an answer, you," that is to say Alija Izetbegovic, "should go on television and say that there is no offensive against Vitez by the BH, in the BH, and we're not children after all. As Ivo says, some people have more experience than others in life. Some are wiser, some are more gregarious, others speak less and do more, et cetera. It's clear to us that strategically for the BH army, Vitez is the most important, as is Novi Travnik, because as my namesake said, there we have capacities for 20 years." Now I'm going to skip over the next portion and carry on with Kljuic's other proposal: "First of all because of the international community, I want you to say we don't have an offensive going, and, secondly, just between us, let's stop the offensive by the 18th -- or until the 18th. Let's see whether that agreement will happen. You will go there for talks and you'll see. Thirdly, let me say that if we expel the few Croats left from this -- from this enclave, then all of us Croats who are for B and H will be defeated because we won't have a people." Dr. Jurcevic, do you know that there was a clash at one point between the BH army and the HVO in Central Bosnia and more specifically in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was one the partial conflicts between the BH units and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What we've just quoted as being the plans of the Bosniak Muslim leadership, does that correspond to what you knew about the actual events on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here on the basis what we've just read, the minutes from the session of the Presidency, it is clear that Novi Travnik and Vitez were of immense importance because of the combat materiel that could be produced there, and it was obvious that according to their concept the views of the Bosniak Muslims, their structures, that not only the HVO but also the civilians were not desirable there and an option that was being put forward here is to open this valve and to let them leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, please look at the next document, which would be 4D930. It's the transcript of a session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is the 14th of January, 1994. I think that the Prlic Defence and the Petkovic Defence have already used this document, but let us try and look at a part that I don't think we have discussed so far. The page is 3/3 in the Croatian text. In the English text, it's the part that ends at page -- or, rather, page that ends with 272. Again it's a statement or part of an intervention by Alija Izetbegovic. It begins at the previous page, but let me focus on this part, and I quote: "Our solution -- this solution with the three republics were imposed on us with the presence of a strong army which doesn't want any other option, and the international community is not ready to remove them from those territories, and it is our assessment that we cannot remove it ourselves." Dr. Jurcevic, can you tell us what army is Mr. Izetbegovic referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably the HVO, if we're talking about this area, the same area that we've just discussed. It's not clear from the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, this document pertain to the plan for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be organised as three republics, and it says here that the solution with three republics was imposed on us because of the presence of one strong army that don't want anything else.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 14th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the eve -- on the eve of the preparations for the Washington Agreements, and by this time, the USA has been involved he very actively here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us read that through.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What terrain are we talking about, what territory?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will follow -- I will follow on with the quote: "I went toward Kosevo hill today and people told me that there are Chetniks in those houses."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please. It should be repeated every ten minutes, because nobody seems to care really.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to monitor the transcript, and I will try and do a better job in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So let me continue with the quote. So there is mention of Chetniks, and it's only about 200 metres in distance: "They have been here for about a year and a half already or when we go toward the airport we pass through a Chetnik check-point. We cannot remove it. Can we remove that army? That is the problem. The presence of that army with 600 to 700 tanks, 2.000 artillery weapons, and approximately 100 to 150.000 soldiers in the field that refuses to have any other solution forces us to think -- to consider whether we should be doing else." Now, Dr. Jurcevic, can you tell us now with an army President Izetbegovic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the technical data, it is obvious that he was speaking about the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really wonder whether someone is listening to what is said from the Bench. Now you have been overlapping all the time. You must wait, Witness, until the translation is over, and then answer it. And you must wait until the translation is over. I know it's difficult. You have temperament and all that, I can really sympathise. Maybe in the same situation, I'd fall into the same trap, but please use your time to your benefit. If we lose half of it, you lose it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor, let us try and be really good and behave. Well, my colleague Mr. Kovacic tells me that the doctor is behaving but that I'm not. So I'll try to behave. So you told us that it is clear now what the army was, and now my question to you is: In the context of this intervention by Alija Izetbegovic, can you comment and say how come that the Bosnian Muslim leadership was considering and accepting the solution that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be set up as a compound state. What is the cause of all that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic concept of the most powerful structure within the Bosnian -- Bosniak Muslim ranks was to have a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. However, the circumstances that evolved, if I may say, forced their hand, forced them to take part in talks, and because the actual situation in the field, they had to accept other solutions, and this follows from what we've just read here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned the unitary state, and now I would like to ask you a couple of questions about the concept of the unitary state as the opposite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you address that topic, Professor, the more we move on in this trial, the more we are exposed to a variety of documents, and I understand that all of this is extremely complex. A while ago we saw a document of the 4th Corps, which was a very clear document. It explained that it is not through diplomatic means that we will find a solution to the problem. The solution is of a military nature. This is what the document seemed to be saying. And now in this document Izetbegovic assesses the military situation, and he says the Serbs have 600 to 700 tanks, 2.000 artillery pieces and 100 to 150.000 men on the ground; so as far as he was concerned, he felt it was impossible to win that battle. On the Muslim side, we see, therefore, that there are diverging views. Mr. Praljak was, a few weeks ago, in your seat. He explained Izetbegovic's and Halilovic's positions. They did not always share the same view. In light of the trial of strengths and the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic spells this out, do you think that there was a likelihood of being able to solve this issue through or by using force, or do you think this could be resolved through diplomatic means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, if I may, this synthetic presentation, I will try to make it as clear as possible. With the break-up of Yugoslavia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina the key problem was how to maintain Bosnia and Herzegovina as a single state. The dominant structures in the Bosniak Muslim side were in favour of keeping Bosnia and Herzegovina together as a state; but as part of their solution, they tried to achieve the greatest possible benefits for their people, their component, and they advocated a unitary state because they were in the majority, and they were the only people that was growing demographically, and by dint of having a unitary state, the constitutive mechanisms that were in place until 1990 would be cancelled out, would no longer apply. A part of the Bosniak Muslim structure did not agree with that, and they distanced themselves from the SDA and from the ruling structure. The second constituent people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats, were also in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina continuing to exist, but they favoured the concept of compound state, which would, by way of respecting their interest as the people in the absolute minority, which also was demographically decreasing, in some part or some several parts would be granted the right of subsidiary government or governments. The third constituent people, the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or their dominant structures, openly, and by all means at their disposal, didn't want to have that part that was emerging at the Republika Srpska to be part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they wanted that to become part of the State of Serbia. So these were the basic concepts and the basic problems and we know what happened as part of all that within that framework. You asked me for my opinion, and it is my opinion -- well, you asked me whether it was possible to achieve a diplomatic solution. Theoretically, of course it was possible, and it was possible in practice had the international community applied the mechanisms that it had at its disposal. And as time went by, from 1991 or the spring of 1992, the conflict escalated. The problems became more complex, and that includes the Bosniak Muslim conflicts, and the end game in 1995 showed that, showed that the possibility of a diplomatic solution diminished day by day. Your Honour, I don't know if you're happy with my opinion. If you are not, please ask me some follow-up questions, because your question was synthetic in nature and very complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having summed this up. I will give the floor back to Mrs. Alaburic while letting her know that she has 13 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note please insert 100 to 150.000 men, instead of 100 to 150. It said 13 minutes, not 30. I --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I continue, I have one question. If I needed some ten minutes to wrap up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. It's working.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I needed ten more minutes to wrap up all the topics I wanted with Dr. Jurcevic, would you allow me to use the ten minutes from the -- this piece abstracted to the time that was allotted to General Petkovic's Defence case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put the question to the other members of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will be given ten extra minutes, but this will be taken off of the overall time that has been given to the Defence team, and Petkovic team. You have 23 minutes left, so try and finish around 12.00. That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in answer to his Judge -- His Honour's question, you said one thing that I find very interesting, and that is that the Muslims as a majority people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although they did not have the absolute majority, preferred the unitary system in Bosnia and Herzegovina; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I did explain why basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let us talk about this topic of unitary versus compound system using the former Yugoslavia as an example. Doctor, can you tell us which peoples in the former Yugoslavia, or what people was more in favour of a unitary or more centralised state system?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about the whole of Yugoslavia, then again, and that's only logical, it would be the Serbian people, which was the most numerous people in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, all the other people in Bosnia or, rather, in Yugoslavia, did they prefer a unitary system or a compound federal system?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not only in Yugoslavia but in -- in general terms. If you have a compound state or a compound community, those who are in the minority, one of the mechanisms of protection that they have is to have a compound state. It is a mechanism to protect their interest. Not minority interest but interest. It is very important within a state system. If you have a unitary state, then it is only logical, and also on the basis of the experience not only from Yugoslav past but the history of other compound states such as the Soviet Union, it is quite obvious that all the other mechanisms, the unitary mechanisms, would make it possible for the majority people to dominate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Doctor, to the best of your knowledge can it be considered that the party that is in favour of a unitary system of a community is a greater patriot than those who are in favour of a compound or federal system in that very same community?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not only my opinion. I would say that this is the prevailing opinion, and it's even a value as -- as the principle of subsidiary, not only when it comes to states but when it comes to various other forms of social relation, the principle of subsidiarity, that means delegating some powers to some other elements and also some protective mechanisms given the complexity of the community, it is a democratic civilisational standard from the point of view of human rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, you spoke about the League of Communists of Yugoslavia yesterday as being an integrative factor in the former Yugoslavia. So I'd like to ask you now about that integrational factor in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, the League of Communists in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it a factor of integration there too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. In similar fashion as was the case when we look at Yugoslavia as a compound community, with the proviso that it ceased in 1990 after the elections to be a factor to be reckoned with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the basic mechanism was within the League of Communists which had -- which acted as a factor of integration? What was it that was an important factor there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constituent character of the three nations, if you're referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and federalism at the level of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, cadres policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other republics, was that under the control of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the League of Communists in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did it take care to see that there was an equal representation of all the nations, not only the three constituent nations but all the other ethnic groups living on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was one of the conditions for maintaining stability in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Doctor, with the disappearance or disintegration of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and, therefore, of BH as well, was it necessary to find new factors of integration in Bosnia and Herzegovina to make things viable?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, and they were, indeed, found, or they became such and gained legitimacy after the results of the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the Croatian leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it want Bosnia-Herzegovina to be established as a federal state like the former Yugoslavia was, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Which Croatian leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina? The witness, in his report, goes on at some length about the -- the Croatian -- Bosnian Croat positions being diverse, heterogeneous, mixed, not the same; so which Croatian leadership is counsel asking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, could you ask the witness to clarify or clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will, but before that, let me ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, tell me, do you know how much of the BH population were Croats at the first democratic elections in 1990? Or, rather, which Croats from Bosnia voted for the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vast majority, and the HDZ, on the basis of that secured I think it was 44 seats in parliament in the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me be more precise, Doctor. When I say the Croatian leadership, I mean that leadership, which at those first democratic elections, won the mandate to set up the local and central government. Can you answer in that way? So the Croatian leadership --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Is she talking about the HDZ leadership under Stjepan Kljujic that was elected in 1990 and was head of the party? Which Croatian leadership are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please clarify, Mrs. Alaburic. There are different Croatian leaderships. It's important to know which one you mean exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to remind you that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded at the time when Mr. Kljujic was the president of the HDZ. So that, from its very inception -- yes, that's right, he was president of the HDZ, and, therefore, we cannot speak about any difference of views or separation of ways amongst the politicians who were ethnic Croats and occupied leading positions at the time when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, perhaps the witness has a different point of view. You said one cannot talk about diverging views. That is your point of view. But what about the witness? The professor, perhaps he has a different point of view. You were anticipating his answer. Put the question to him and ask him. According to him, what are the names of the important Croatian leaders, those from the HDZ, and streamline your question, otherwise Mr. Scott will get to his feet again and there's no getting out of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in lines 5 and 6, your question to me was recorded as saying that it was necessary to know what I mean when I say the Croatian leadership, so that my explanations were not leading questions suggesting the answer but a clarification and in a way a response to Mr. Scott who mentioned Mr. Stjepan Kljujic. So I think that my question is sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Dr. Jurcevic, is my question sufficiently clear as far as you're concerned, or do you need me to be more precise and tell you which people and structures I mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. I don't think that the essential question is whether the question is clear to Mr. Jurcevic. The essential question is whether it's clear to the Bench, and I can associate myself with the question of Judge Antonetti and I'm a bit amazed that you seem to have answered in such an evasive way. Which leadership? The leadership under Mr. Kljujic or some other strata. I think that should not be a problem to answer clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I, on the other hand, consider that if there is any difference then this expert witness can tell us: Under Stjepan Kljujic, that's how it was; under Mate Boban, when he was president of the HDZ, this is how it was; and I think that as far as this expert witness is concerned, who has explained the events to us according to the different periods and gave us a lot of nuances in his qualifications, I don't have to specify my question in that way. Were we dealing with a witness who was not well-acquainted with the political events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then I would feel it necessary to ask him whether he feels the HDZ leadership in 1991, 1992, or some other year was as it was; but in view of everything that the witness has told us here, I really don't think that I have to specify to him, and that if there are any difference, he would not be able to answer and tell us what the differences are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Jurcevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still disagree. We cannot pretend that the witness has not given us a 190-page report in which the witness goes on for some pages about the HDZ BiH being diverse, having being heterogeneous, not having the same views and that the faction -- a particular faction prevailed ultimately by the end of 1992, which was different from the leadership in 1990. Now, he can't ignore that. That's his report. So which Croatian leadership is Ms. Alaburic talking about, the ones that were elected in 1990 or the ones that existed at the end of 1992 or whatever date she's talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I think that Ms. Alaburic has a bit clarified that she wants the witness to give a differentiated answer, and let's see what we get.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then my last comment, and I apologise, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My last comment would be: Can we, once again, specify time. What time-frame are we specifically talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Dr. Jurcevic, will you know who I mean if, when I say Croatian political leadership, I have in mind people who as representatives of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina took part at international negotiations on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not related to the names of the particular people. When you say authorities, you mean the structures that be. Of course, the structure's also a dynamic body, but as a structure, it persists and has a power. And in view of the heterogeneous character, it is quite clear that a structure also existed regardless of its changeable character, and the most important thing is that there was a dominant structure and one of the attributes of dominance was participation in international negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that we were talking about a unitary and compound state. And in view of that, I'm going to ask you the following question: What kind of Bosnia-Herzegovina did the representatives of the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina advocate during the international negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, why it is so difficult to ask who he's talking? This man has talked to us for two days now. He claims to have great knowledge of these events. He's written a long -- why can't he tell us and why can't counsel be more clear in saying which Croatian leadership is he talking about. We're going around and around, and I suggest to the Chamber it's not by accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are well-versed in all these events. When one reads your report and your footnotes, all the articles you have read, you followed up on all the trials here. Since you are aware and knowledgeable about a number of things, you do know that there were rifts between a number of individuals among the Croatian leadership. You know there were diverging views, and the Prosecutor states it and says it again and again. So this is something we know. What would be useful would be if you could tell us, No, the Croats all agreed from Boban to Kljujic that they wanted a unitary system. Or you say, No, there were diverging views and they did not all agree. And then you say who is who and what is what. This is what the Prosecutor would like to hear and this is what the Bench would like to hear also because we are not as specialised as you are in this field. Even if we have been sitting as the Bench of this trial for the last four years, we've heard a lot of witnesses, we've read a swathe of pages, but I don't claim to have the same level of knowledge as you do. So please try and give us some more detail about the names of these people. This is what we would like to elicit from you. Is this something you can do or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I think that even with the explanations -- with the explanations, it would take up too much time. Now if the question was the structures which took part and represented the Croatian side at international negotiations, then that's a very clear question and the answer is simple. But the processes of heterogeneity within the Croatian national body and within the structures is quite another matter, quite another question; and I think we're dealing with a question of principle here, at least that's how I understood it. If it is not the case, then please tell me, but anyway, at the negotiations and in other political matters in BH, especially those under international supervision, there is a continuity in advocating this question of principle on the part of the most dominant section of the population represented in the structures. Of course there were individuals who changed their position depending on their motives, circumstances, and other interests; however, I understood that this was a question of principle because we were discussing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that Mrs. Alaburic did talk about the issue of representation of Croats in international negotiations, and you're saying that they represented without a single voice at the time. Maybe, but was part of the political ideas of Croats in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina excluded from the single voice? And could you tell us which Croats were not included in the political negotiation and when. We know that Mr. Kljujic at first was president of the HDZ and then there's going to be a problem. This is what we're trying to understand thanks to you. We know that there will be Mr. Boban in Geneva, but according to you, does Mr. Boban represent the political ideas of the Croats in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at a hundred per cent or only at 70 per cent or 40 per cent? We'd like to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The structure was -- well, the Croatian structure in BH was advocated and represented by different individuals, but when we talk about the organisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, then in the ruling structure, it was dominant, although in other structures, too, that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be a compound state. For example, when the structure from Herceg-Bosna advocated a certain unit from which other parts of Croats in central BH and Posavina, they were against -- when they stepped down, they were against the structure precisely because they were excluded from that compound state or, rather, for not participating in the entity which was Croatian. That is to say that would be protection for them or, rather, they would be afraid of not being protected by that entity. So the explanation lies somewhere along those lines. So indubitably without a doubt even with the problem of the referendum and all the international plans, there was continuity on the part of the Croatian national interest, which, despite its heterogeneous character and because of other matters and considerations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Jurcevic, but really to the question which was asked by the President, by Judge Antonetti, you are giving a rather long but very general answer. What was asked from you, what is your position and answer and reply concerning Mr. Boban's position or others' position. Did Mr. Boban's position represent 70 or 40 per cent of the -- of the Croats over there, et cetera. So please kindly try to give us a quite-to-the point answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having been asked this concrete question, if it relates to a particular detail, it's impossible to answer because when the situation is changing from one minute to the next in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was no research into public opinion nor was any kind of referendum held where the Croats could, as individuals, as the population, state their views about these issues. The only relevant indicator and indices were the elections held in 1990, and they lent legitimacy to that dominant structure allowing them to represent certain interests. I concluded that they were represented by this structure very poorly, and I stated my reasons. Apart from that, I also said that it was a highly unstable structure and that only within that Croatian structure were there great cadres changes afoot. And by way of arguments, I said that only in the Croatian structure and at the head of the HDZ you had frequent changes as opposed to the other two structures where there were no such changes. And so at the level of my expert report, that is an important indicator. And it is also common knowledge that several weeks after -- or, rather, before the elections, after the establishment of the HDZ, the first president was replaced, Mr. Perinovic. The next person that came along was Kljujic, and at the end of 1994, we see a situation where Kresimir Zubak headed it. So in these dramatic circumstances with such frequent changes at the number-one post, the number-one party post, leading the post, which according to the elections of 1990 was only structure to have legitimacy this testifies to the lack of stability and heterogeneous character of that same structure which certainly harmed Croatian national interests or harmed the Croats and the Croatian national interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because this lack of stability, once it is linked up with the general instability in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the contradictions coming from the international community, the problems and -- and stratification within the Muslims structures themselves, it is quite clear what this is about defined at that level. And in this regard, it would be very difficult in view of the complexity of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina generally now, and it's not relevant for the level that I followed in my expert report, what the personal motives and interests were, or the interests of some smaller group and very often they could be identified and equated to some material interests or some other security considerations or personal interests or something else, why they changed their opinions and why they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you. If we understand correctly, you're saying that at the level of the structure of the HDZ, the HDZ was quite heterogeneous and the best proof of this is that there were changes at the head of the HDZ, and you mentioned three names, saying that the last one, Zubak, for example, had been dramatic. We understand that. So as far as you're concerned, you believe that the HDZ was a very heterogeneous party. However, the HDZ was not the sole party in the Geneva negotiations, if I'm correct. I think that there was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. There was also a person called Mate Boban. So as far as the Croatian council of Herceg-Bosna is concerned, whose founding text was in Grude, was this a monolithic structure or was this also a very heterogeneous structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The structure in Herceg-Bosna, in the Croatian Community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as you have noted yourself was, of course, heterogeneous; and we could see on some specific documents of military origin, and that goes also for the civilian relations, that you could see this heterogeneous character and that the mechanisms of power did not change. So localism and all other various interests were dominant within the community and the Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So the heterogeneity was present at all levels, and today on the basis of some documents that show that subordinate unit quite simply refuses to obey an order from the Main Staff. But when we're talking about the structure in international relations, well, they were always the first to sign up. They did not make any conditions, and they did not renounce their signatures, unlike the other two sides, the Serb side and the Bosniak Muslim side which were much more cohesive internally. And all the situations, including the international plans, were seen in a different way. They made demands, then signed and then renounced the signatures at times, and sometimes even finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor. With the ten additional minutes, you have 13 minutes left. So we could stop at 12.30 for the break, of course if we have no further objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, this -- we will deal with the same topic but using a different methodology. Can you tell us very briefly whether Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time was a unitary or a compound state? At this time, now. So I'm correcting the interpretation. So is Bosnia and Herzegovina today a unitary or a compound state?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a specific form of a compound state.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And this form of organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a compound state, is it something that international community put forward in Dayton?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community tabled it and then imposed this solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the course of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the international community ever table a proposal for the future organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina that would not entail it being a compound state?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the proposals on the part of the international community, and I think are all public and publicly known, were such that the -- that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be a compound community.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did Alija Izetbegovic, on behalf of the Muslim side in the negotiations, ever refuse a proposal put forward by the international community with the justification that what he wanted was a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Clearly. Not conclusively but clearly rejected a proposal giving this reason as a justification.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Although you can, of course, interpret things in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have time for interpretations. Could you please tell us the names of prominent Croatian politicians in Bosnia and Herzegovina who advocated a unitary system in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Are you aware of anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it's difficult to give their names. Again, you could interpreter -- well, on the basis of some statements given at some point in time you could speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me move on to my next topic and that's the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And now I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your last question is not -- your answer, I'm sorry, is not quite clear to me. You say you can speculate about that. Does that mean that you cannot say positively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I couldn't say that categorically that a prominent Croat politician did advocate that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at 4D1349. It's the first proposal, the proposal tabled by the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia. So this is how the international community proposes to resolve the Yugoslav crisis. This document, are you familiar with it? Did you see it at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And in item 1.1(a), it says that the Yugoslav crisis will be resolved in such a way that sovereign and independent republics with international personality for those that wish it will be established, and in item (e) it says that there would be recognition of the independence within the existing borders, unless otherwise agreed, to the republics -- to those republics who wish again. Can you tell me on the basis of this document what were the basic positions of the international community when it came to creating independent states from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was consistently stated by various institutions of the international community. There were two basic criteria. The first was not to recognise any changings -- changing of the borders achieved by force, and the second was consistent respect for human rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jurcevic, in your opinion, Franjo Tudjman and the leadership of the Republic of Croatia, were they aware of the fact that the moment Bosnia and Herzegovina becomes an independent internationally recognised state, it would be recognised as such within it's borders as they were defined by AVNOJ, in other words, the borders of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it was within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was clear to Tudjman and to others who participated in that, and Tudjman, I think, had some additional reasons not to tamper with the AVNOJ borders anywhere in particular, not in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because that would be introducing the criterion into this whole situation in the former Yugoslavia for the parts of the Republic of Croatia that had been occupied to achieve recognition. And it was clear, furthermore, the international community stated that several times, that it would not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That was my second question. So the leadership of the Republic of Croatia was aware of the fact, or do you know whether it was aware, that it was impossible to change the borders by force? So in any other way but by an agreement of all the interested parties?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was absolutely aware of that. And perhaps just one additional fact. The Republic of Croatia, realistically speaking, did not have the military force that it would need to change the situation, and you can see that from the fact that it was only in 1995, that it was able to carry out an operation to liberate its territory; and it was only in 1988, because of a lack of political and military strength, it agreed to a very, very problematic process of the reintegration -- peaceful reintegration of the Danube basin in the eastern part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, we don't have time to address this issue about the borders of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because I would like us to look at 4D1453. It's our next document. It's a transcript of the testimony by Professor Smilja Avramov. She teaches international law at the Belgrade University. She's a professor there, and she was one of the key advisors to the Serbian President, the late Slobodan Milosevic. It's a separate document, so it's not in the binder. It was attached thereto because it's a voluminous document. And now I would like to draw the attention of the Judges to the pages, relevant pages, and I will rephrase and paraphrase what Smilja Avramov said. So 32412 is the page for Your Honours, through 414, and then page 32428 and 32436, and then we will comment on that later on. In the initial pages, Smilja Avramov speaks about the testimony about Stjepan Mesic about the events Karadjordjevo, labelling this testimony as nothing but lies; because at the meaning between Milosevic and Tudjman, no borders were drawn, borders between Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then she goes on to explain how the scholars in Serbia considered the AVNOJ borders to be revolutionary borders which have not been internationally recognised, and that if Yugoslavia were to break down those borders could not be internationally recognised in any way. And they tell me that the transcript has stopped. All right. The important thing is that we have the central transcript working. Let me quote a sentence which is important because Croatia is mentioned. It's at page 32413. The end of the penultimate paragraph, she says: [In English] "My position was that only these international treaties could be the basis for future borders with which the Croatian side did not agree." [Interpretation] And these are the treaties that follow the Second World War -- or, rather, the First World War in 1919 and 1923. And then on page 32428, she says: [In English] "The borders remain open if Croatia and Slovenia insist on seceding, then there is the possibility that Serbia would accept this but under one condition, that we use peaceful means to decide upon the question of borders." [Interpretation] End of quote. And then and then at the last page that I mentioned, Smilja Avramov says this -- that halfway down the last paragraph: [In English] "On the 18th of October, without any preparation, without any previous information, I was informed 24 hours beforehand. We received the so-called Carrington paper, which puts to us the distinct disintegration of Yugoslavia without any alternatives." [Interpretation] I'll skip a couple of lines: [In English] "They accept it, revolutionary principles, you see. They accepted states within the borders that were established during the revolution, the AVNOJ borders which was unacceptable for us." [Interpretation] If we recall the document that we have just seen, that would be the Carrington paper that was issued on the 18th of October. Now, Dr. Jurcevic, tell us can you comment in this context on the position taken by the Serbian leadership, in particular Slobodan Milosevic, and the leadership of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, on the AVNOJ borders. Let me be more specific in my question because -- so I'm asking you about the difference regarding the position of the AVNOJ borders, and I would like to apologise to the interpretation. Their interpretation was correct.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The differences were so large that it's, in fact, a contradiction. The Serbian side, headed by Milosevic, and the whole structure advocated the changing of the borders and the Croatian state, headed by Franjo Tudjman, insisted on the AVNOJ borders, of course, each because of their own interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jurcevic, I will have to interrupt you because I have very little time. I have unfortunately completed this part. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just say what we've prepared. My colleague Ms. Senka Nozica and I prepared three documents which would show to you the use of fonts today in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you would see that the designation of the state Bosnia and Herzegovina in those documents is done in a smaller font than the text that follows in those documents. So since you, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, expressed an interest in this question whether the size of the font is -- goes beyond the graphic design of a document, has some other meaning, I would like to just show you those three documents and then you can give appropriate weight to the size of the fonts, if you allow me to do that. But I would like us to move on into private session, because the documents that Madam Nozica gave me - and I would like to thank you for that - are private documents. So to protect the identity of the persons who are mentioned in those documents, perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break for 20 minutes. Then Mr. Karnavas will have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and again good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor. Now, I want to turn to your report, which for the record is 3D03720, and I'm going to ask you to look at page 129, that is in your language; and for us it would be page 109, 109 would be the English version. And when you -- 129. And when you have it, let me know. For the purpose --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say, 129 what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will provide it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could guess the assistance of the usher right now, we could move along quicker. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I want to focus your attention to one particular paragraph. For us in English, it would be the second paragraph starting with, "Prior to this on May 22, 1993," and in parentheses you say: "Only three days after the failure of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan (five members of the and UN Security Council)(France, the Russian Federation, Spain, the UK and the US) had issued a joint statement on the BH expressing a their 'profound concern' over the continuation of clashes in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And it goes on. So what I want to do, Professor, is focus on the first part of this paragraph, the first line, in fact, where you say: "On 22 May 1993, only three days after the failure of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan." Now, over the weekend we did have a chance to meet, did we not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in during period of time, I asked you concretely if you were aware of any negotiations or agreements that came out of Medjugorje on or about that period of time. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you -- I want to share with you 1D02404. You should have it there. Everybody should have it. Its been distributed. 1D02404. We've seen this document before or various of it. This exhibit. It's an exhibit. Now, were you aware of the existence of this particular document at the time that you were preparing your report and came to -- and made that assertion about the death or the end of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I didn't use it in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, having looked at this, at Exhibit 1D02404, would you like to take the opportunity now to perhaps either amend your assessment or comment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can comment on it. As it says here in the introduction and the methodology part of my expert report, I, in fact, made a synthesis which consistently followed a certain level when it came to the international community and Bosnia-Herzegovina in that chapter, and when it comes to the peace agreements, then I followed them in such -- until they fell through as an integral solution for BH. I didn't enter into the level of bilateral agreements between two of the parties, because then in all other -- I would have to look at all the other cases and then my expert report would be longer. So this agreement, if I am allowed to comment, relates to two sides, two parties, in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say the Croatian and the Muslim Bosniak side. And this document, in fact, shows that those two sides, despite the fact that an integral solution for BH fell through on the 19th of May after having been rejected by the Serb side after the referendum, it was, in fact, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan that a part of the international community took part and that resulted in this particular agreement, and they worked on it for some time to come. So that this document testifies to the fact that part of the international community, although the plan failed, did continue its initiative and attempted to apply it. And certain structures from Bosnia and Herzegovina took part in that process including the Croatian and the Muslim Bosniak side, and they acted under the leadership of part of the international community, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just to make sure that I'm crystal clear, would I be correct, would we be correct, in understanding your assessment that at least with respect to those individuals that were involved in this particular agreement and wherever they were representing, the Vance-Owen Peace Plan had not failed at that time, and, in fact, they were making efforts to implement it to the extent as is reflected in this particular agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They continued to act in keeping with the plan which the Serb side rejected. When I say the plan failed, what I meant was that it failed as an integral solution for the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because if one party, in this case the Serb party, rejected it, that meant that it fell through as an integral solution. But obviously it wasn't a failure from the aspects of the other two sides, not in my opinion, but also according to the opinion of the international community -- or, rather, that portion of it which took part in an attempt to implement the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, my next topic, and this will be my last topic, if we could move to another document, and this is Exhibit 1D02961, 1D02961. This is a document that was first discussed through a previous witness, and I can provide the information for the record if that is necessary. If you could just look at this document first. And again over the weekend when we met, I did, in fact, show you this document, and you had a chance to look it over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is fully correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we'll discuss the text in a minute, but first if we could look at this document. Toward the end, we see that there are some symbols. And the B/C/S page at the end is 1D580046, but you'll be able to see it. We're looking at the symbols because this has been somewhat contentious in this particular trial. Now, do you recognise these symbols and, if so, can you please tell us what are they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's appeared on our screens. It is the coat of arms and flag which was used on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, are they the same as those used in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They're similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we can see from this document that it was generated in 1997. And have you had a chance to look at part of the text, especially with respect to the part that talks about the historical background, and given -- and for your purposes, it would be on page -- if you look at the bottom, it will be 1D580047.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A summary of the study of the Croatian Community. Yes, I have looked at the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, because of your background, I suspect that you would be qualified to give us an opinion, an expert opinion, as to the correctness of this particular overview and, if so, could you please share that with us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, it is a customary amateur report or study which in similar forms and similar circumstances is used in Croatian social life, not only during this period but prior to that as well, and in similar documents like statutes for various associations and organisations and the like, it was customary to quote or to put it into some historical context to give it more weight, but this was an amateur work altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: By and large, can you give us an opinion as to the quality of it? I know you said it's amateur, but is it -- is it more or less accurate? Do you find anything that's glaringly inaccurate from a historical point of view, in light of your background that is.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing special. Certain fragments have been taken. Three pages of text going through the whole of history, taking certain fragments from the different periods of history, and they're not structured in a scholarly or scientific way, neither are they very deep. So it's a superficial, amateur piece of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if we look at the beginning of this document, we see there is a statute, that is the statute of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and as I've indicated, we see that it's dated -- it has a date of 24 May 1997 as to when it was passed. And, of course, you having been a historian, being from the region and also knowing the events, it would be fair to say that at this period of time when this statute was at least adopted by those who adopted it, Bosnia and Herzegovina was under international care, if I could put it that way. It's a benevolent way of saying that it was governed by the Office of the High Representative, OHR; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in way today, too, was under the dominant and decisive supervision of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, the OHR, or the High Representative, I should say, has not hesitated in the past to either dismiss political figures who after being elected if in any way they were in violation of either the spirit or the letter of the Dayton Peace Accords. You're familiar with that, are you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would even say that unusually for Europe in a radical way, without any explanations. Some individuals were stripped of their rights and very radically so in certain circumstances on the part of the OHR or High Representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to share with you one last document, and that is Exhibit 1D03148, 1D03148.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For Your Honours, we just translated the most relevant part. We can translate the entire document if you wish. This document we received from the Office of the Prosecution, so it's their document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at this very quickly and look at the first part. It would appear, would it not, that the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in 1997, as the statute shows, including the -- the flags and the coat of arms attached thereto, were, in fact, registered officially and approved by the powers that be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would also include the Office of the High Representative. Does this not reflect that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that -- that you don't challenge that. We can speculate, of course, but anyway, the powers that be did their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one last question: Those flags and that coat of arms, is it not a fact that those are not symbols that came into being in the last 5 or 10 or 15 years but actually go back, much further back in history, perhaps centuries?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both the coat of arms and the flag are symbols which were used and which were created over history in a similar form, and they were used from the 1990s; but generally speaking, from the 1990s, they represent something that we can call folklore, symbols of general usage used on occasions of this kind when organisations are being set up or associations and are used if daily life too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But this is for Croatia or for Bosnia and Herzegovina? Just to make sure that we're clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These symbols here, the ones we have. You mean the coat of arms and the flag; right? And as I said, they are similar. Similar coats of arms have their historical source on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, this graphic design with the squares, but, yes, these were used in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions. I want to thank you very much for coming here to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Scott, we have half an hour left. Can you start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd be pleased to. It will take a moment to organise ourselves and pass out the binders, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Interpreters have not received any binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I see that the interpreters are saying that they have -- haven't received any documents. I know that it was a huge amount of work for you to prepare all these binders, and I thank you for that because they have been well prepared as they always are; but admittedly, had you been able to give the translation booths a binder as well, this would make their work easier, and it's easier for them to follow. This is something which would be nice to have. It's a wish on my part, but it is not an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm certainly not in a position to be able to create additional binders in a short time, and that is in the three and a half years that has not been the practice. I have no doubt that it would be helpful to the translation booths who -- all of whom have my great thanks for the good work they do, but we have not prepared on that basis. We've acted consistently with the pat three and a half years of practice on that. Hopefully, if there's a particular issue, we can try to assist as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps we can start by --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance with the ELMO. Unfortunately, we will have to remove, I think, some of the materials there. It may be helpful to have another other trolley or something there. If I can ask the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe we can just start on the note of just recognising your presidential candidacy. Is that a poster or board that has been prepared in connection with your candidacy for president of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Counsellor, thank you for promoting my candidature. Yes, this is one of the promotion posters or the customary type of poster that you see in Croatia's political life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And perhaps the blue text beneath the red line, if you will, can you just tell us what that -- help those of us who don't speak Croatian, what that says?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says -- well, my name first, first name, last name, Josip Jurcevic. Under that it says on the red band, "Croatian President," and then underneath that in blue, "When, if not now!"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, now, just touching on your background. We've see how far we can get this afternoon before, obviously, continuing into tomorrow. I understand that you graduated --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That can be taken down, usher. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand from your CV which has been marked as 3D03725; which should be in the first binder if anyone cares -- wishes to look at it at the moment, I believe. Yes. Sir, you've indicated that -- we know that you graduated with a degree in history and philosophy --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think you should advise the witness that this [indiscernible] number is his expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, his CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 3D03725, sir, that was a copy of your CV that was provided to us by Mr. Praljak's counsel. We've already talked about the fact you graduated with an undergraduate degree in history and philosophy in 1975, and then, sir, you tell us in your CV on the second -- I believe, it's on the second page under employment, and I'm not trying to be unkind, but just to put your total testimony in context, you say yourself that from 1975 to 1991 you had no steady employment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And not before that either, because I was studying then, and I gained full employment in 1994, towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. And in 1991, according to your CV, you went to work at the Croatian Ministry of Defence as the founder and director of the Croatian Ministry of Defence Central Archives; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first day I responded to a question from the Bench, and I spoke about that in greater detail. So in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the -- excuse me, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I was a volunteer --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My time is very limited, and I will tell you that now to be as courteous as possible. I'll ask you to give very short answers. If you can possibly answer my questions yes or no, please do so. If you ramble on, with great respect, sir, I'm going to cut you off. My question is very simple. You went to work at the Ministry of Defence as the founder and director of the central archives in 1991; correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't give yes or no answers to certain questions, because then the Court will -- or you will extract from me a simple answer but the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on your CV --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it would be more exact to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not -- listen to my question, please. We're going to get started on the right foot here. We're not going to do this. Your CV says, does it not: "1991-1992, Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, founder and director of the Croatian Ministry of Defence Central Archives." It says that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us how given your -- your track record, so to speak, of no steady employment in the previous 16 years, how did you come to have that particular position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have described that in part. I described it to Their Honours yesterday, but if need be, I can give you all the details too. I was one of the founders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who hired you? Who hired you? Who was the individual who gave you or made it possible for you to have that job?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a permanent job. That's number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether it was permanent or not. Who gave you the job? Sir, our time limited. Listen to my question. Please answer my question. I would greatly appreciated it. Who gave you that job?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was enabled to do that job by the Main Staff of the Ministry of Defence, the Main Staff of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was that, sir? Who was the individual, the human being who gave you that -- made that position possible for you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an individual, it was an institution. My unit was the only unit dealing with the gathering of material, and when it decided to set up a -- when the archives were decided to be set up, then they employed me and a whole unit to be a sort of central archive, but that's the story apart, because it was not an archive that was formally registered. And there is a detailed explanation about that in the Gotovina trial where I responded and said I would testify about the archive and how it came into being, and I provided the Court with a written explanation of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, sir. That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was employed by an institution, not an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you indicated yesterday or -- yes, yesterday, that there was one individual between you -- in terms of supervision of the hierarchy, if you will, that there was one individual between you and Mr. Slobodan Praljak. Can you identify who that individual was, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the archives or the IPD administration, then it was its head, but that head changed. And when the archives were established and upon my arrival and taking up this status, Mr. Praljak still was not the assistant minister or in charge of this, but the person is deceased, Anton Mijatovic. The other person is living, and he's Ante Mulacic [phoen], and the third person who came later was Ivan Tolj. They were the heads of that particular department administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also told us that during this time, in fact, you worked for something called the department for information and psychological operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the department for information, you had seven parts. One was the central archives of which I was, in formal terms, the founder and director.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- but from what you told us yesterday, sir, your work there did not -- was not exclusively working on the archive, and, in fact, you were somewhat dismissive of your work on the archive, and you at least gave me the impression, I'll give you a chance to correct it, but you were really primarily engaged in other things; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I don't know how you gained that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is the department for information and psychological operations, is that sometimes referred to as the IPD?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I note in your CV that there seems to be a gap, unless I've missed it, but again under the section of employment. 1993 seems to have gone missing. Can you tell us what you were doing after -- between 1992 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unemployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You joined the Ivo Pilar, excuse me if I mispronounce that, Institute of Social Sciences in 1997 and you've been there continuously to the present time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have been in a full-time job there since that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any current position or title that's associated with your employment there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am a leader of a functional centre for research into peace, war, and on terrorism, and I am a senior scientific associate. That's my official job title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who is your superior at the institute, please, in terms of who you report to or take direction from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In scientific terms, I am responsible to the Ministry of Science which approves various projects, and the administrative director of the institute is Dr. Vlado Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Sakic is another person who will be an expert witness for Mr. Praljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He has a doctorate in psychology, and he specialised in social psychology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you refer to the Ministry of Science, that's the Ministry of Science of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, directly or indirectly, sir, essentially you work for the Government of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP JURCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a public institute, and it is part of the Ministry of Science and Education of the Republic of Croatia, which means that it is part of the state public system like all the other primary, secondary schools, universities and so on, because that's the system in Croatia.
